tooltip.title: Morphology + site + recurrence + systemic context
tooltip.markdown: Describe number, size, border, base, depth, keratinized versus nonkeratinized mucosa, gingival involvement, preceding vesicle, healing/scar, and extraoral findings before ordering tests.

tooltip.title: Common phenotype
tooltip.markdown: Usually <1 cm, 1–5 ulcers, nonkeratinized mucosa, heals in 7–14 days without scar. Diagnosis is clinical after excluding secondary causes when the pattern is new or atypical.

tooltip.title: Broaden workup
tooltip.markdown: Larger/deeper ulcers, prolonged healing, scarring, near-continuous disease, genital ulceration, or systemic symptoms. Evaluate Behçet syndrome, IBD, hematologic disease, immunodeficiency, nutritional deficiency, and drug causes.

tooltip.title: Fresh lesion testing
tooltip.markdown: Grouped vesicles/erosions on keratinized mucosa or vermilion support recurrent intraoral HSV; PCR from a fresh lesion is preferred when confirmation is needed. Consider CMV, syphilis, deep fungal disease, and bacterial causes in the appropriate host.

tooltip.title: Biopsy with DIF
tooltip.markdown: Desquamative gingivitis, widespread fragile bullae/erosions, chronic mucosal disease, ocular/genital involvement, or skin blisters suggest pemphigus, MMP, erosive lichen planus, linear IgA disease, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, or lupus.

tooltip.title: Chronology
tooltip.markdown: NSAIDs, nicorandil, methotrexate toxicity, mycophenolate, cytotoxic therapy, mTOR inhibitors, checkpoint inhibitors, and other agents can cause ulceration or lichenoid/immune-mediated disease.

tooltip.title: First separate an ulcer from an erosion or blister
tooltip.markdown: Recurrent aphthous ulceration is common, but persistent, atypical, multisite, scarring, ocular, genital, systemic, or immunocompromised presentations require a broader rheum–derm, infectious, hematologic, and malignant differential.

tooltip.title: Aphthous pattern
tooltip.markdown: Round/ovoid painful ulcers with a fibrinous base and erythematous halo on nonkeratinized mucosa. Classify minor, major, or herpetiform; ask about frequency, healing time, scarring, triggers, nutritional status, GI symptoms, genital ulcers, and eye disease.

tooltip.title: Autoimmune/infectious pattern
tooltip.markdown: Pemphigus vulgaris, mucous membrane pemphigoid, erosive lichen planus, lupus, erythema multiforme, HSV, and other disorders may present as erosions rather than a primary aphthous ulcer. Two biopsies may be required for H&E and DIF.

tooltip.title: Pattern clusters
tooltip.markdown: Behçet syndrome, SLE, IBD, reactive arthritis, neutropenia, cyclic fever syndromes, celiac disease, nutritional deficiency, HIV, and medication toxicity are selected associations.

tooltip.title: Biopsy threshold
tooltip.markdown: A solitary ulcer persisting beyond approximately 2–3 weeks, induration, fixation, unexplained bleeding, cervical adenopathy, high-risk exposure, or progressive pain requires prompt biopsy to exclude squamous cell carcinoma and other neoplasia.

tooltip.title: Escalate
tooltip.markdown: Ocular inflammation, airway compromise, inability to hydrate, severe neutropenia/fever, widespread mucosal detachment, suspected malignancy, or genital/ocular scarring disease.

tooltip.title: The accompanying organ system narrows the diagnosis
tooltip.markdown: Aphthous morphology alone is not enough to diagnose Behçet syndrome or lupus.

tooltip.title: Behçet syndrome
tooltip.markdown: Recurrent oral ulcers are nearly universal, but diagnostic weight comes from genital ulceration/scarring, uveitis/retinal vasculitis, papulopustular or erythema-nodosum–like skin disease, pathergy, vascular thrombosis/aneurysm, neurologic or GI involvement.

tooltip.title: SLE/CLE
tooltip.markdown: Lupus ulcers may be painless and involve the hard/soft palate junction; oral discoid lesions and lichenoid plaques can occur. Interpret ANA/ENA/complement with the systemic phenotype.

tooltip.title: IBD/celiac/nutritional
tooltip.markdown: Crohn disease can cause deep linear ulcers, cobblestoning, lip swelling, and mucosal tags. Aphthae may accompany either Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis. Check iron, B12, folate, and celiac testing when clinically indicated.

tooltip.title: Neutropenia and marrow disease
tooltip.markdown: CBC with differential is high-yield for abrupt severe aphthae, fever, recurrent infection, chemotherapy exposure, cyclic pattern, or systemic illness.

tooltip.title: Reactive arthritis / spondyloarthritis
tooltip.markdown: Oral erosions are often shallow and painless; examine palms/soles, genital mucosa, nails, and joints.

tooltip.title: Treat cause, pain, and function
tooltip.markdown: Management begins with oral hygiene, avoidance of trauma/irritants, pain control, and correction of an identified trigger; systemic therapy should match the diagnosis and organ risk.

tooltip.title: Stepwise
tooltip.markdown: Topical corticosteroid is first-line; topical anesthetic and protective agents support intake. For frequent/severe disease, colchicine or another systemic steroid-sparing option may be considered after secondary causes and contraindications are addressed.

tooltip.title: Domain-based
tooltip.markdown: Topical corticosteroids for individual ulcers; colchicine or apremilast are common systemic options for recurrent mucocutaneous disease. Eye, vascular, neurologic, or GI disease requires organ-specific immunosuppression.

tooltip.title: Specialist-directed
tooltip.markdown: Potent topical corticosteroids may control limited oral disease, but systemic glucocorticoid-sparing therapy is often required. MMP needs prompt ocular, laryngeal, esophageal, and genital review because scarring can be irreversible.

tooltip.title: Targeted therapy
tooltip.markdown: Use antivirals, antibiotics, or antifungals only when the organism and host context support the diagnosis; avoid escalating immunosuppression in an unrecognized infection.

tooltip.title: Maintain nutrition and oral health
tooltip.markdown: Salt/bicarbonate rinses, bland diet, soft toothbrush, dental care, treatment of candidiasis, and nutrition/hydration support. Avoid alcohol-containing rinses and traumatic products.
